subject: chemistry
title: Enthalpy Comet: ΔH and Hess Cycles
welcome_lead: Trace the energy flow of reactions using enthalpy and Hess's law.
meta_desc: A-Level chemistry adventure on enthalpy changes and Hess cycles.
final_note: You have mastered energy bookkeeping in reactions.

walkthroughs.body_html:
To find ΔHr from ΔHf values: ΔHr = Σ ΔHf(products) - Σ ΔHf(reactants).

To find ΔHr from ΔHc values: ΔHr = Σ ΔHc(reactants) - Σ ΔHc(products). Always include states and multiply by stoichiometric coefficients.

ΔH ≈ Σ bonds broken - Σ bonds made. Bonds broken = endothermic (+), bonds made = exothermic (-).

Bond enthalpies are mean values, so this gives only an estimate. Works only when all species are gaseous.

q = m c ΔT. For solutions take m as the solution mass and c as 4.18 J/g/K.

ΔH per mol = -q / n (negative because exothermic releases heat to surroundings). Heat loss to surroundings makes measured values less exothermic than true.

mcqs.q: In an exothermic reaction, what happens energetically with the bonds?
options: Energy released forming new bonds exceeds energy absorbed breaking existing bonds.
All endothermic reactions are spontaneous at room temperature.
The reactants get colder because they lose mass as energy.
Bond breaking releases energy and bond making absorbs energy.
Hess's Law works because reactions can only happen in one specific direction.
Enthalpy is a state function — change depends only on initial and final states, not the route taken.
The reactants get colder because they lose mass as energy.
Hess's Law works because energy always cancels out around any cycle.

mcqs.q: Why can an endothermic reaction still be spontaneous?
options: Hess's Law works because reactions can only happen in one specific direction.
All endothermic reactions are spontaneous at room temperature.
Endothermic reactions are never spontaneous because they require energy input.
If the entropy increase (TΔS) is large enough to outweigh the positive ΔH, ΔG can still be negative.
